answer_text: Fort Laramie was established by the American Fur Company, which well-nigh monopolized the Indian trade of the whole region. Its officials ruled there with absolute sway, and the arm of the United States had little force — when Parkman was there, the extreme outposts of American troops were about seven hundred miles to the eastward (Chapter VIII, "Scenes at Fort Laramie").

Hand-wrought silver spoon - Veblen's illustration: some ten to twenty dollars
Machine-made aluminium spoon - Veblen's illustration: some ten to twenty cents

The hand-wrought silver spoon is priced at ten to twenty dollars, while the machine-made aluminium spoon costs only ten to twenty cents — roughly a one-hundred-fold difference in value.

The Island - starting population: about seven millions
The Island - after fifty years (two periods of twenty-five years): population twenty-eight millions; means of subsistence equal to the support of twenty-one millions

Malthus starts from a population of about seven millions; after fifty years the population would be twenty-eight millions while the means of subsistence would support only twenty-one millions, a shortfall of seven millions.

Yes, force is allowed in the bridge case as described. Per Chapter V (Applications), if a public officer or anyone sees a person attempting to cross a bridge ascertained to be unsafe and there is no time to warn him, they may seize him and turn him back. This is no real infringement of his liberty because liberty consists in doing what one desires, and he does not desire to fall into the river. However, when there is not a certainty but only a danger of mischief, no one but the person himself can judge the sufficiency of the motive for incurring the risk, so (unless he is a child, delirious, or in some state of excitement or absorption incompatible with the full use of the reflecting faculty) he ought only to be warned of the danger, not forcibly prevented. Per Chapter I (Introductory), the doctrine does not apply at all to children or young persons below the age the law fixes as manhood or womanhood—those still requiring care by others must be protected against their own actions as well as external injury.

Veblen concedes that the corset impairs the wearer's personal attractions, but this loss is offset by the gain in reputability that comes from her visibly increased expensiveness and infirmity (Chapter Seven, evidence [1]).

The corset is a mutilation undergone to lower the subject's vitality and render her permanently and obviously unfit for work, serving as evidence of honorific leisure by arguing physical disability (evidence [1], [2], [4]).

It has fallen into disuse among the richest class because a large enough leisure class has grown up with such wealth that any aspersion on the score of enforced manual employment would be idle and harmless calumny (evidence [5]).

It persists among wealthy groups that are exceptions to this rule: the wealthy classes of countries with a lower, more archaic industrial structure, and later accessions to wealth in advanced industrial communities who have not yet had time to divest themselves of the plebeian canons of taste carried over from their former lower pecuniary grade—for example, higher social classes of American cities that have recently and rapidly risen into opulence (evidence [4], [5]). Veblen says the corset persists through the period of snobbery, the interval of transition from a lower to an upper level of pecuniary culture (evidence [4]).

1st edition (1859) - assumptions: breeds when thirty years old, breeds till ninety years old, bringing forth three pair of young in this interval
1st edition (1859) - result: at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair
6th edition (1872) - assumptions: begins breeding when thirty years old, goes on breeding till ninety years old, bringing forth six young in the interval, and surviving till one hundred years old
6th edition (1872) - result: after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair

Between editions, Darwin changed the assumption from three pair of young to six young in the breeding interval and added that elephants survive till one hundred years old; the result changed from fifteen million elephants at the end of the fifth century to nearly nineteen million elephants after 740 to 750 years.

Darwin calls it the doctrine of Malthus applied to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms [1][2][5][6]. In Malthus's own essay, population when unchecked increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio [3]. Based on the United States experience, Malthus takes as his rule that unchecked population doubles itself every twenty-five years [4].

Mill - On Liberty: social tyranny, the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling, which penetrates much more deeply into the details of life and enslaves the soul itself [1].
Tocqueville - Democracy in America: public opinion and the majority's control of all avenues of redress—opinion, legislature, executive, troops, jury, and even elected judges—so the wronged individual must simply submit [4].

Difference: Mill stresses society's moral/psychological reach into the soul, while Tocqueville stresses the majority's institutional and opinion-based grip that leaves no means of redress.

Malthus's rule - 1798 Essay: population, when unchecked, doubles every twenty-five years (geometrical ratio).
United States population - 1790: 3,929,328.
United States population - 1830: 12,856,165.
Tocqueville's statement - Democracy in America: the population, nearly 4,000,000 in 1790, had more than tripled in the space of forty years, amounting to nearly 13,000,000 in 1830.

The figures bear Malthus out: 3,929,328 doubled twice (×4) would be about 15.7 million, and the actual 1830 figure of 12,856,165 (more than tripled) is consistent with roughly a 25-year doubling period. Tocqueville himself gives a doubling period of about twenty years, since the population more than tripled in forty years.

On Liberty - Mill: the feeling of the majority, to whom any appearance of a more showy or costly style of living than they can hope to rival is disagreeable, operates as a tolerably effectual sumptuary law, making it difficult in many parts of the Union for a person with a very large income to find any mode of spending it that will not incur popular disapprobation.
The Theory of the Leisure Class - Veblen: the accepted standard of expenditure in the community or class largely determines a person's standard of living, enforced through popular insistence on conformity to the accepted scale of expenditure as a matter of propriety, under pain of disesteem and ostracism.

Mill describes majority feeling in the United States acting as an effective sumptuary law that restrains conspicuous spending by the wealthy; Veblen's theory explains the restrained motive as the desire to display a showy or costly standard of expenditure beyond one's rivals, which society checks through disesteem and ostracism for nonconformity.
